title: The Gijon Rule

primary_metric: the ceiling: the larger of two percents of the 49 Algeria-Chile result cells (0-6 goals each) in which West Germany and Austria are still sure to go through, for a 1-0 West Germany win and for a 6-5 West Germany win; lower is better for the committee

The 0-6 goal window, the 49-cell grid, the 'safe/unresolved' definitions, the two benchmark scorelines and the steerable-scoreline simplification are the author's counting method (MA1-MA4), not facts about football.
Option B as a rule (goals scored before goal difference) is a hypothetical; it was not adopted.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Every match in the grid is limited to 0-6 goals per side, giving 49 Algeria-Chile cells

modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value; see sensitivity_disclosure[].

modeling_assumptions.assumption: An unresolved tie for the last qualifying place is never counted as safe

sensitivity_note: SPEC section 6 does not apply to death, illness or hardship, but the case concerns a real match and real teams: it is framed as an incentive-structure story, never an accusation. FIFA ruled no rule was broken; the case never alleges match-fixing.

balance.argument_a: Option A has the lower ceiling: 42 of 49 cells (85.7%) for the best benchmark scoreline against Option B's 45 of 49 (91.8%), so B is 7.14% worse on the primary number. A is also what FIFA actually did, rewrites no 1982 result, and goals-first does not remove the cooperative scoreline, it moves it: under B the safest scoreline becomes a high-scoring win (6-5), so two teams that both profit could cooperate on a goal-fest, and B changes the incentives of every future group, for every team (a side protecting a lead gains nothing from goal difference, attacking play is rewarded whether or not it wins).
balance.argument_b: Option B cuts the 1-0 gamble, the scoreline actually played in 1982: it is safe in 29 of 49 cells (59.2%) under B against 39 of 49 (79.6%) under A, and the whole 10-cell drop comes from the Algeria-win cells (11 of 21 down to 1 of 21). Applied to 1982 as played, B would have sent Algeria through instead of Austria. B's safe set for 1-0 is a subset of A's, so it removes cells without adding any. B's cost is bounded: only one of the five other 1982 groups changes (Group 6: Scotland replaces the Soviet Union). On the average of the two benchmark percents (a summary staff also report and the committee has not ruled out), Option B is lower: A 82.7% against B 75.5%, so A's average is 9.46% higher. Honest note: on the ceiling as defined, B loses (7.14%); B's case needs the argument that one extreme scoreline (a 6-5 match, eleven goals) should not outvote the scoreline actually played, so the case is balanced only because the choice of summary (ceiling or average) is left open in the Background.
balance.margin_basis: Ceiling = max over the two benchmark scorelines of (safe cells / 49); margin = (B ceiling - A ceiling) / A ceiling = (45-42)/42 = 7.14%, favoring Option A. Recomputed in sensitivity_model.py.
balance.twist_effect: Late information that Algeria-Chile ended as a narrow Algeria win (by one or two goals; 11 of 49 cells, re-based per Appendix C/MA6; the as-played 3-2 is inside the set). A is safe at both benchmarks in 11 of 11 cells (ceiling 100%, average 100%); B is safe at 1-0 in 1 of 11 and at 6-5 in 11 of 11 (ceiling 100%, average 54.5%). The ceilings tie, A's 7.14% lead vanishes, and the average gap widens sharply in B's favour; neither option becomes obviously correct because the choice now turns on which summary the committee adopts and on D5 (unchanged costs). Follow-ups: Algeria not winning (28 cells) ties everything at 100%; Algeria won (21 cells) keeps A's ceiling lead and B's average lead. Disclosed here and in sensitivity_model.py; never in case.md.
balance.stability: The ceiling comparison depends on the goal window (MA1): at 0-3 goals the ceilings tie (15 of 16 cells each), at 0-6 A is lower by 7.14%, at 0-9 A is lower by 19.23% (inside the 20% cap). Disclosed in sensitivity_disclosure[].

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1 is a counting-window choice with no real-world value to research. Flexing -50% (0-3 goals) makes the two ceilings tie (15 of 16 cells each); flexing +50% (0-9 goals) widens Option A's lead to 19.23%, still inside the 20% cap. Disclosed as an irreducible modelling choice, not a researchable figure.

deliverables.text: A Group 2 standings table (matches played, points, GF, GA, goal difference) as it stood when West Germany-Austria kicked off, with every goal-difference subtraction including negatives, then the as-played update by signed addition and what separated Algeria.

The three-point test: for every scoreline in the 0-6 window in which West Germany scores more than Austria (21), with Algeria-Chile fixed at 3-2, the advancing pair under two and under three points per win, marking any unresolved scoreline, and whether any pair differs.

Option A: the number of Algeria-Chile cells by the Fundamental Counting Principle, two filled grids (1-0 and 6-5) marked safe / not safe / unresolved, with counts, percents and the split by Algeria win/draw/loss.
Option B: the same two grids, plus a Venn diagram of the safe-cell sets under A and B for 1-0, with region counts and a statement of whether one set is a subset of the other.
The cost to history: the advancing pair in Groups 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 under the 1982 ladder and Option B's ladder, every group whose pair changes, and Group 2 as played under Option B.

The recommendation: the ceiling and the average (percents) for each option and their comparison; a short written recommendation using Outcome and Event on why coasting is individually rational, what each option costs, and the number that would change your mind.

context_glossary.desc: A team's goals scored minus the goals scored against it across its matches. It can be negative. In 1982 it was the first test used to separate teams level on points.
A rule used to separate teams that are level on points. A ladder of tie-breaks is applied one test at a time until one of them gives different answers.
A schedule in which every team plays every other team once. A four-team round-robin has six matches.
The moment a football match starts. Two matches with the same kickoff time are played at the same time, so neither team can wait to see the other result.

catalog.ask: A rules committee must decide whether simultaneous kickoffs alone are enough, or whether goals scored should also come before goal difference. The answer turns on which scoreline two teams could still rely on, and what the fix costs every other group.
